title: Fossilised dinosaur dung
keyIdea: A coprolite is fossilised dung: animal poo that was buried fast and slowly turned to stone. Scientists cut thin slices or scan coprolites to see inside. Bits of bone mean a meat-eater, wood, seeds or leaves mean a plant-eater, and fish scales mean a fish-eater. A coprolite 44 cm long from Canada was full of bone from a young plant-eating dinosaur, so a big meat-eater, most likely T. rex, made it. Clues give a best guess, not a sure answer, because nobody saw who did the poo.
familyTip: Next time you see animal droppings on a walk, ask: what did this animal eat? Look for seeds, fur or bits of shell, without touching. Then ask how sure you are, and what would make you surer. If you visit a museum, look for coprolites in the fossil cases: many museums have one.

visual.caption: What did the animal eat? Drag each coprolite, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: turn poo into stone in order, cut a coprolite open, sort coprolites by diet, measure one, and decide how sure we can be.

kid: A coprolite is poo that turned to stone. It is a kind of fossil. The poo had to be covered by mud very fast. Then, over a very long time, minerals soaked in and made it hard. It does not smell now.

Scientists cut a coprolite into thin slices, or scan it, to look inside. They find tiny bits of what the animal ate. Bone means it ate meat. Wood, seeds or leaves mean it ate plants. Fish scales mean it ate fish.

In Canada, scientists found a coprolite 44 cm long. It was full of broken bone from a young plant-eating dinosaur. A big poo full of bone came from a big meat-eater. T. rex was the big meat-eater that lived there.
But nobody saw it happen. A poo has no name on it. So scientists say T. rex “most likely” made it. They use clues to make a best guess.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. The word coprolite comes from Greek: kopros means dung and lithos means stone. William Buckland coined it in 1829. Mary Anning had noticed that odd stones found inside ichthyosaur skeletons at Lyme Regis held fish bones and scales when broken open. The lesson fits the National Curriculum in England: Year 3 rocks and fossils, and the Year 6 idea that fossils give evidence about life long ago.

Dung only becomes a fossil if it is buried fast, before it rots or is eaten. Minerals then fill it and replace it. Meat-eaters’ dung is kept more often, because the phosphate from bone helps it harden. Scientists cut thin slices or use scans and microscopes. Inside they find bone, plant tissue, seeds, pollen, scales and even worm eggs. In 1998 Karen Chin and her team described a coprolite 44 cm long from Saskatchewan. It was 30 to 50% bone from a young plant-eating dinosaur. Its size, its contents and the animals of that time and place point to Tyrannosaurus rex. In 2007 Chin found rotted conifer wood in dung thought to come from duck-billed dinosaurs.

Common mistakes: thinking a coprolite is still soft poo, or that any dropping left lying about turns to stone; assuming a big dropping means a plant-eater; and treating the maker as certain. A coprolite rarely names its maker. Scientists reason from size, shape, contents and which animals lived there, and they say “most likely”.

In the lab your child orders the steps from fresh poo to stone, cuts a coprolite open and names the bone, seed, wood and fish scale inside, sorts coprolites by diet, measures the 44 cm coprolite on a ruler and picks its likely maker, and sorts claims into what we can say and what is too sure.

practice.hint: Copro means poo. Lite means stone.
practice.explain: A coprolite is fossilised dung: poo that was buried fast and slowly turned to stone.

practice.prompt: A coprolite is {n} cm long. Another is {k} cm longer. How long is the second one, in cm?
practice.hint: Start at {n} cm and add {k} cm.
practice.explain: {n} cm and {k} cm more make {=n+k} cm. A longer coprolite usually came from a bigger animal.

practice.prompt: A coprolite has fish scales inside. What did the animal eat?
practice.hint: Where do scales like that come from?
practice.explain: Fish scales and fish bones mean the animal ate fish.

practice.prompt: A scientist cuts {n} slices from one coprolite and {k} slices from another. How many slices is that?
practice.hint: Count the slices from the first one, then count on.
practice.explain: {n} slices and {k} more make {=n+k} slices to look at under a microscope.

practice.prompt: Why must dung be covered fast to become a fossil?
choices: So it does not rot or get eaten first
So it can dry in the sun
practice.hint: What happens to poo that is left lying about?
practice.explain: Dung left out rots, crumbles or gets eaten. Covered fast by mud, it can slowly turn to stone.

pool.prompt: A big coprolite is full of broken bone. Who most likely made it?
pool.hint: Big tells you the size. What does the bone tell you?
pool.explain: A big meat-eater. Size points to a big animal, and the bone shows it ate meat.

pool.prompt: How do scientists see what is inside a coprolite?
choices: Cut thin slices or scan it
pool.hint: A coprolite is hard stone. How do you look inside a stone?
pool.explain: They cut thin slices to look at under a microscope, or scan it without cutting.

pool.prompt: A coprolite has rotted wood and seeds inside. What does it tell us?
choices: Nothing: it is just a rock
pool.hint: Where do wood and seeds come from?
pool.explain: Wood and seeds come from plants, so a plant-eater made it.

pool.prompt: Can scientists be sure which dinosaur did a poo?
choices: No, it is a best guess from clues
pool.hint: Did anyone see the dinosaur do it?
pool.explain: No. Nobody saw it, so scientists use clues and say “most likely”.

pool.prompt: A coprolite is {n} cm long. A ruler is 30 cm long. How many cm longer than the ruler is the coprolite?
pool.hint: The coprolite is longer than the ruler. Find the difference: take the ruler’s 30 cm away from {n} cm.

pool.prompt: Which comes first when poo becomes a coprolite?
pool.hint: What must happen before it can rot or get eaten?
pool.explain: First mud covers it fast. Then minerals soak in for a very long time, and it turns to stone.

pool.prompt: The 44 cm coprolite from Canada was full of bone from a young plant-eater. What does that tell us?
choices: A big meat-eater ate a young plant-eater
pool.hint: Whose bones were inside, and who eats bones?
pool.explain: A big meat-eater, most likely T. rex, ate a young plant-eating dinosaur.

pool.prompt: A slice shows {n} bits of bone and {k} fish scales. How many bits is that in all?
pool.hint: Add the bone bits and the fish scales.
pool.explain: {n} and {k} make {=n+k} bits. This animal ate fish and other bony animals.

pool.prompt: Who first saw fish bones and scales inside these stones at Lyme Regis?
pool.hint: She was a famous fossil hunter on the coast of England.
pool.explain: Mary Anning noticed them. William Buckland then named them coprolites in 1829.

pool.prompt: Which one can a scientist say about a coprolite full of bone?
choices: It was T. rex for sure
pool.hint: Only say what the clues show.
pool.explain: The bone inside shows the animal ate bone. The name and feelings are not shown.
